notes: Synthetic runbooks for a retrieval quality golden set. Fictional systems and commands only. Hard cases on purpose: near-duplicate pairs (r02/r03, r05/r06), a superseded version (r18), a withdrawn runbook (r19), a near-identical runbook in another workspace (r20) and a long runbook whose answers sit in later chunks (r17). v2 adds r21-r26: pairs of runbooks that differ mainly by an identifier (SQLSTATE 53300/53400, max_wal_size/wal_keep_size, Redis OOM/LOADING).

runbooks.title: PostgreSQL primary failover
runbooks.body:
# PostgreSQL primary failover
Use this when the primary database stops accepting writes and health checks fail for more than two minutes.
1. Confirm replication lag on the standby is below 5 seconds before you promote it. A larger lag means recent writes would be lost.
2. Promote the standby to primary with the fictional command `dbctl promote --standby ledger-db-2`.
3. Repoint the connection pooler to the new primary and reload it; applications reconnect on their own.
4. Fence the old primary so it cannot accept writes if it comes back, then open a ticket to rebuild it as a standby.
Record the promotion time and the observed lag in the incident timeline.

runbooks.title: Restore the incident database from a nightly backup
runbooks.body:
# Restore the incident database from a nightly backup
Nightly logical dumps of the incident database are kept for 30 days.
Before restoring, verify the checksum of the dump file against the manifest written by the backup job. Never restore a dump whose checksum does not match.
Restore into the staging environment first and run the integrity checks there.
A production restore needs a recorded approval from the incident commander.
For point-in-time recovery, replay the WAL archive up to the timestamp just before the bad change.
After the restore, compare row counts of the incidents and runbooks tables with the last known good report.

runbooks.title: Restore attachment files from object storage snapshots
runbooks.body:
# Restore attachment files from object storage snapshots
Incident attachments live in the attachments bucket, not in the database. This runbook does not cover database restores.
The bucket keeps object versions for 14 days. To recover a deleted or overwritten attachment, list the object versions and copy the last good version back over the current key.
For bulk recovery after accidental deletion, restore the whole prefix from the daily bucket snapshot into a quarantine prefix first, scan it, then move the files back.
Tell the reporters whose attachments were affected once the files are back.

runbooks.title: Renew an expiring TLS certificate
runbooks.body:
# Renew an expiring TLS certificate
The monitoring alert fires when a public certificate expires in fewer than 14 days.
Request a new certificate through the ACME client with the fictional command `certctl renew api.ledger.example`.
Store the new key only in the secret store, never in the repository.
Reload the ingress so it serves the new certificate without dropping connections.
Verify the full chain from outside with `openssl s_client -connect api.ledger.example:443 -servername api.ledger.example` and confirm the new expiry date.

runbooks.title: Rotate database credentials
runbooks.body:
# Rotate database credentials
Rotate the password of the application database role every 90 days or immediately after a suspected leak.
Create the new password for the ledger_app role and write it to the secret store as a new version.
Roll out the API pods one at a time so each pod picks up the new database password from the secret store.
Keep the old password valid for 24 hours, then revoke it and confirm no connections still use it.

runbooks.title: Rotate third-party API keys
runbooks.body:
# Rotate third-party API keys
This covers keys for external providers such as the payment processor and the email service, not database passwords.
Generate a new key in the provider dashboard and add it next to the current one: the integration accepts two active keys during a dual-key window.
Switch traffic to the new key, watch the provider error rate for an hour, then delete the old key in the provider dashboard.
If a key leaked, delete it first and accept a short outage of that integration.

runbooks.title: Free disk space when a volume is nearly full
runbooks.body:
# Free disk space when a volume is nearly full
The alert fires when disk usage on a data volume goes above 90 percent.
First find what grew: application logs, temporary export files and old core dumps are the usual causes.
Force a log rotation and delete compressed logs older than seven days.
Remove export files in the temporary exports directory that are older than one day.
If usage is still above 85 percent, expand the volume online and file a capacity ticket.

runbooks.title: Investigate a worker memory leak
runbooks.body:
# Investigate a worker memory leak
Suspect a leak when the resident memory of the background worker grows steadily across hours and the container is OOMKilled and restarted.
Take a heap snapshot from one affected worker before restarting it; a restart erases the evidence.
Compare two snapshots taken ten minutes apart and look for object counts that only grow.
As a mitigation, restart workers on a schedule while the fix is prepared, and lower the batch size.

runbooks.title: Drain a growing job queue backlog
runbooks.body:
# Drain a growing job queue backlog
The queue depth alert fires when more than 5000 jobs are waiting for over ten minutes.
Scale the worker deployment out to the maximum of twelve replicas.
Pause non-critical producers such as report generation so urgent notification jobs drain first.
Jobs that fail three times move to the dead letter queue; review them after the backlog clears instead of retrying them blindly.

runbooks.title: Roll back a faulty deployment
runbooks.body:
# Roll back a faulty deployment
Roll back when the error rate or the share of 502 responses rises sharply within 30 minutes of a release.
Redeploy the previous image tag recorded in the release log with the fictional command `deployctl rollback api --to previous`.
Freeze further deployments until the cause is understood.
Database migrations are not reverted automatically: check whether the release ran one and whether the previous version can run against the new schema.

runbooks.title: Disable a feature with its kill switch
runbooks.body:
# Disable a feature with its kill switch
Every new feature ships behind a flag that can switch it off in production without a deployment.
Set the feature flag to off in the flag service; the change reaches all API instances within 60 seconds.
Confirm in the flag audit log that the change was recorded with your name and the incident number.
Leave the flag off until the owning team signs off on a fix.

runbooks.title: Diagnose DNS resolution failures
runbooks.body:
# Diagnose DNS resolution failures
Symptoms are clients that cannot resolve service hostnames, with NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL answers.
Query the authoritative servers directly to tell a missing record apart from a resolver problem.
If a record was changed recently, remember that resolvers keep the old answer until its TTL expires.
For SERVFAIL, check whether DNSSEC signatures on the zone have expired.

runbooks.title: Handle clients hitting the API rate limit
runbooks.body:
# Handle clients hitting the API rate limit
Clients over their quota receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.
Identify the client from the API key in the rate limiter dashboard and check whether the traffic is a retry storm or real growth.
A temporary quota increase needs approval from the service owner and expires automatically after 48 hours.
Tell the client to back off exponentially and honour Retry-After.

runbooks.title: Escalate a severity 1 incident
runbooks.body:
# Escalate a severity 1 incident
A severity 1 incident means customers cannot use a core feature.
Page the incident commander on call within five minutes of declaring it.
Open a dedicated bridge call and a channel named after the incident number.
Post an update on the status page every 30 minutes, even when there is nothing new to say.

runbooks.title: Atender una solicitud de exportación de datos personales
runbooks.body:
# Atender una solicitud de exportación de datos personales
Una persona puede pedir una copia de todos sus datos personales guardados en el sistema.
Primero verificá la identidad del solicitante con el procedimiento de doble confirmación por correo.
El plazo legal para responder es de 30 días corridos desde la solicitud.
Exportá los datos en un formato legible por máquina, como JSON, y enviá el archivo por el canal seguro.
Registrá la solicitud y la fecha de entrega en el registro de privacidad.

runbooks.title: Mitigar una avalancha de caché tras un vencimiento masivo
runbooks.body:
# Mitigar una avalancha de caché tras un vencimiento masivo
Si muchas claves del caché vencen al mismo tiempo, todas las peticiones van a la base de datos a la vez y la latencia se dispara.
Activá la coalescencia de peticiones para que una sola consulta regenere cada clave.
Agregá una variación aleatoria al TTL de las claves para que no venzan juntas.
Si la base de datos sigue saturada, serví temporalmente los valores vencidos mientras se regeneran.

runbooks.title: Quarterly disaster recovery drill
runbooks.body:
# Quarterly disaster recovery drill
This drill proves that the team can rebuild the incident ledger in the secondary region from backups alone. Schedule it once per quarter and announce it one week ahead.

## Preparation
Pick a drill lead and a scribe. The scribe keeps a timestamped log from the first command to the last check.
Confirm that the latest nightly dump and the WAL archive have been replicated to the secondary region. If replication is behind, postpone the drill: it would measure the replication delay instead of the recovery.
Prepare an empty environment in the secondary region with the same versions of PostgreSQL and pgvector as production.
Agree on a fictional bad change to recover from, for example dropping one table at a known time.

## Execution
Apply the bad change in the drill environment and note the exact time.
Restore the nightly dump, then replay the WAL archive to the moment just before the bad change.
Rebuild the knowledge index for every published runbook so semantic search works again.
Start the API and the worker against the restored database and run the smoke checks.
Do not touch production at any point during the drill.

## Objectives
The recovery time objective is four hours from the start of the restore to passing smoke checks.
The recovery point objective is fifteen minutes of lost writes at most.

## After the drill
Record the measured recovery time and the measured recovery point in the drill report, next to the objectives.
List every manual step that was not in this runbook and every command that failed.
Open a ticket for each gap and assign an owner before closing the drill.
Destroy the drill environment so it does not keep restored data around.

runbooks.title: Clear stuck background jobs
runbooks.body:
# Clear stuck background jobs
Jobs are stuck when they stay in the running state long after their timeout.
Run the fictional command `jobctl delete --stuck` to remove the rows from the jobs table and let producers create them again.

revision.body:
# Clear stuck background jobs
Jobs are stuck when they stay in the running state long after their timeout.
Use the fictional command `jobctl requeue --stuck` to move them back to the queue with their payload intact.
Never delete rows from the jobs table directly: producers do not recreate deleted jobs, so their work is silently lost.
If a job gets stuck again after requeueing, move it to the dead letter queue and open a ticket.

runbooks.obsoleteEvidence: remove the rows from the jobs table

runbooks.title: Reboot the whole cluster to fix latency
runbooks.body:
# Reboot the whole cluster to fix latency
When latency is high, reboot every node of the cluster at once to clear all state.
This guidance was withdrawn because it causes a full outage.

runbooks.title: PostgreSQL primary failover (South region)
runbooks.body:
# PostgreSQL primary failover (South region)
Use this when the South primary database stops accepting writes.
Confirm replication lag on the South standby is below 5 seconds, then promote it with `dbctl promote --standby south-db-2`.
Repoint the South connection pooler and fence the old primary.

runbooks.title: PostgreSQL error 53300: too many connections
runbooks.body:
# PostgreSQL error 53300: too many connections
Use this when clients fail with SQLSTATE 53300 (too_many_connections) and the message "sorry, too many clients already".
1. Count sessions per application in pg_stat_activity; idle in transaction sessions are the usual cause.
2. Do not raise max_connections first: every connection costs memory on the primary.
3. Route the API pods through PgBouncer with pool_mode=transaction and a default_pool_size of 20.
4. Terminate sessions idle in transaction for more than ten minutes with pg_terminate_backend.
5. Record the peak connection count in the incident timeline.

runbooks.title: PostgreSQL error 53400: configuration limit exceeded
runbooks.body:
# PostgreSQL error 53400: configuration limit exceeded
Use this when a statement fails with SQLSTATE 53400 (configuration_limit_exceeded), usually "out of shared memory" with a hint to increase max_locks_per_transaction.
1. Find the transaction that locks many partitions or tables at once; bulk migrations are the usual cause.
2. Split the work into batches that touch fewer partitions per transaction.
3. If the workload is legitimate, raise max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128; it needs a restart of the primary and the standby.
4. Note the change and the restart window in the incident.

runbooks.title: Checkpoints too frequent: tune max_wal_size
runbooks.body:
# Checkpoints too frequent: tune max_wal_size
Use this when the log repeats "checkpoints are occurring too frequently" and write latency spikes every few minutes.
1. Check pg_stat_bgwriter: checkpoints_req much higher than checkpoints_timed means max_wal_size is too small.
2. Raise max_wal_size from 1GB to 4GB and keep checkpoint_timeout at 15min; a reload is enough, no restart.
3. Confirm the WAL volume has room for the larger size before you change it.
4. Watch checkpoint duration for one hour after the change.

runbooks.title: Standby fell behind: requested WAL segment removed
runbooks.body:
# Standby fell behind: requested WAL segment removed
Use this when a standby stops replicating with "requested WAL segment has already been removed".
1. The primary recycled WAL the standby still needed. The standby cannot catch up from the primary alone.
2. Rebuild the standby with pg_basebackup from the primary.
3. To prevent a repeat, raise wal_keep_size to 8GB on the primary, or use a physical replication slot and alert on its retained WAL.
4. A slot with no consumer fills the disk: drop unused slots.

runbooks.title: Redis OOM: command not allowed when used memory exceeds maxmemory
runbooks.body:
# Redis OOM: command not allowed when used memory exceeds maxmemory
Use this when writes fail with "OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'".
1. Run INFO memory and compare used_memory with maxmemory.
2. The cache must evict instead of failing: set maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lru for the cache instance. Never use an eviction policy on the job queue instance.
3. Find large keys with redis-cli --bigkeys and add a TTL to keys written without one.
4. Raise maxmemory only after eviction is in place.

runbooks.title: Redis replies LOADING after a restart
runbooks.body:
# Redis replies LOADING after a restart
Use this when clients get "LOADING Redis is loading the dataset in memory" right after a Redis restart or failover.
1. This is expected while Redis reads its snapshot from disk; do not restart it again, that starts the load over.
2. Check loading_eta_seconds in INFO persistence to estimate the wait.
3. Make the API retry LOADING with backoff instead of failing the request.
4. If loads take longer than five minutes, the snapshot is too large: review key expiry.
